name: Under-eye filler (tear trough)

lead: Tear trough filler is a soft gel, usually hyaluronic acid, placed in the groove between the lower eyelid and the cheek. The payoff people want is a smoother under-eye area with less hollowing and less of the shadow that makes eyes look tired, without lower eyelid surgery.

The filler adds volume under the skin, which camouflages the hollow and the bulge of orbital fat that casts the shadow [1]. Clinicians use it widely as a non-surgical option. A systematic review of 42 articles on hyaluronic acid tear trough techniques found no standardized approach, and a case series of 198 eyes in 100 patients evaluated it as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery. On looksmaxxing forums it is described as a small change that shows in person without looking overdone.

paras: It is done in a clinic by a trained injector, usually as a short appointment with the result visible straight away once initial swelling settles. People often pair it with cheek filler or skincare for the under-eye area. Results from hyaluronic acid filler are temporary and are topped up over time.

Swelling after treatment is common; in one retrospective review of 706 treatments it occurred in over half of patients. Delayed lumps, discoloration and xanthelasma-like reactions are described in a systematic review of delayed complications. Rare orbital events have been reported, including a case of orbital compartment syndrome with bleeding behind the eye that resolved without lasting visual loss [5]. The area is technically demanding, so injector skill matters.

angle.text: Filler fills the tear trough hollow so the shadowing under your eyes softens and the area looks smoother and more rested. The change is visible right after treatment. Reviews describe it as common but technically demanding.

lead: Under-eye filler, or tear trough filler, is the injection of a dermal filler, most often hyaluronic acid (HA), into the tear trough, the depression running from the inner corner of the eye toward the cheek, to soften hollowing and shadowing under the eyes [1][2]. Reviews state that dermal fillers can camouflage tear trough deformity and orbital fat pseudoherniation [1].

A systematic review of 42 articles on HA tear trough techniques found most evidence to be level III, with no standardized, evidence-based approach comparing needle and cannula injection [2]. A case series of 198 eyes in 100 patients, mostly female, evaluated HA filler as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery [3].

Documented complications include post-injection swelling, delayed lumps and discoloration, and rare orbital events [4][5]. Public interest in the procedure is visible in search data: Google Trends analysis found tear trough filler search interest changed by more than 50 percent within single weeks [6].
infobox: Filler injected into the tear trough (infraorbital hollow) [1]
Swelling, nodules, discoloration, rare orbital and vascular events [4][5]
Fillers are FDA-approved medical devices injected by providers [10]

paras: The periorbital region can be treated with neuromodulators, which lift the brow and improve lines, and with fillers, which camouflage the tear trough and herniated orbital fat appearance [1]. A common technique described uses a blunt cannula along tailored linear paths, reported in a series of 1,452 tear trough applications between 2016 and 2020 [7]. Systematic review data found no significant difference in reported aesthetic results between needle and cannula approaches, and no standardised technique [2].

Evidence on effectiveness consists largely of retrospective, non-experimental studies; most of the 42 articles in one review were level III [2]. A consecutive case series of 198 eyes, followed on average 5.1 months, assessed patient satisfaction with an HA filler as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery [3]. Registered trials include a Phase 4 pilot of two HA fillers in the lower eyelid [8] and a study of an HA product versus no treatment for infra-orbital hollows [9].

A retrospective review of 447 patients and 706 infraorbital HA treatments reported swelling in 51 percent of patients not receiving triamcinolone, versus 23 percent when low-dose triamcinolone was mixed with the filler; swelling rose with the volume injected. A systematic review of 52 cases of delayed complications found swelling the most common (42.3 percent), followed by lumps or nodules (25.0 percent) and xanthelasma-like reactions (17.3 percent); 98 percent were female, and HA was the most reported product [4]. A case report described orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage after tear trough filler, treated with surgery with no lasting visual compromise, described as the first such report [5]. Wikipedia describes blindness after fillers as rare but typically permanent [10].

Human research includes systematic reviews of techniques and delayed complications [2][4], retrospective cohorts [7], a consecutive case series [3], and a case report of an orbital complication [5]. Registered trials include a platelet-rich fibrin study for tear trough rejuvenation [11], a two-filler pilot [8] and a study of RHA Redensity Eye versus no treatment [9]. No randomized trial identified here examines under-eye filler for young men seeking an appearance goal.

A looksmax.org user reported having tear trough and jaw filler in one session, described little downtime apart from swelling and said the total cost was $450; replies were mostly mocking or asked for photos [12]. Treatment is described in communities as a small correction that can be noticeable in person without looking plastic.

lore.intro: Under-eye filler appears in forums mainly as personal reports of a minor adjustment rather than a core 'hardmaxx' procedure [12].
